    Scene Around

    Students and faculty with experience in the entertainment industry discuss the complex realities of acting beyond the spotlight.
    By Madison Shen, Harvard-Westlake School • October 28, 2026
    Kendall Clark ’28
    Kendall Clark ’28 poses on the red carpet at Kidz Con.

    A stranger’s eyes catch Kendall Clark ’28, lingering a beat too long as she pushes her cart past Clark in the aisle of her local Ralph’s. Clark notices the stare, but doesn’t think much of it until the woman turns around and walks back towards her. She asks if Clark was on “Grey’s Anatomy.” Clark confirms it, surprised that someone recognized her in public, and watches the woman reach for her phone, asking for a photo before Clark can even respond. For Clark, the moment feels surreal. Having only appeared briefly in the show, Clark said her interaction was one of the few times she has been recognized in public, which she attributes to how rarely she talks about her work.

    “I don’t bring acting up,” Clark said. “I don’t talk about my work that much because it doesn’t feel like that big of a deal to me since I’ve been acting for so long. I’m not in a lot of shows that people our age watch, so people don’t recognize me that often.”

    Clark said she began modeling as a baby, but it wasn’t until she was 5-years-old that she decided she wanted to star in television shows and commercials.

    “I started modeling when I was a baby, and I still model to this day,” Clark said. “I was watching an episode of ‘Jessie’ on Disney Channel when I told my mom, ‘I want to do that.’ My mom made it happen. I started [taking] acting classes, and I got a manager early on, which was lucky.”

    Story continues below advertisement

    For many actors, however, rejection comes more often than success, regardless of experience. It can take up to 99 commercial auditions to book a single job, according to a study conducted by Backstage, an entertainment industry publication.

    53.3% of students said they perceive the entertainment industry to be a glamorous job, according to a Chronicle poll.

    Upper School History and Interdisciplinary Studies and Independent Research Teacher Lilas Lane worked professionally as an actress for over a decade before coming to the school. Lane said navigating rejection required both realistic expectations and a genuine passion for acting.​

    “There’s a lot of rejection,” Lane said. “You’re doing really well if you get one out of 10 jobs. That means nine times you’re getting rejected before you get a job. Actors have to have this ‘I won’t be happy unless I do this’ kind of [mindset] and a willingness to deal with rejection.”

    ​Elliot Murphy ’27, a student actress who has been featured in three short films and 10 commercials, said that rejection rarely has anything to do with talent.

    “I had to learn early on that not getting a role or a callback does not speak to my ability to act, but to what the casting directors and what the production wanted as that character,” Murphy said. “I had to cope with not getting a role I thought was perfect for me because, most of the time, it’s a reason you can’t control that causes you to not get that role. It’s not you being a terrible actress. It’s your hair color, height or something you just can’t change. It’s simply not what directors were looking for at that moment.”

    Working actors scored significantly higher on measures of grit, a psychological trait tied to perseverance and long-term passion, than both student actors and non-actors. Both professional and student actors also scored significantly higher than non-actors on openness, a personality trait tied to curiosity and creativity, according to the National Library of Medicine.

    Clark said staying in the industry has depended on chance and relationships just as much as persistence.

    “When I was seven, I booked my first job as an extra in ‘Stranger Things’,” Clark said. “I got pretty lucky because usually people spend a lot of time auditioning, but the directors liked my look. I got most of my jobs by networking, and I credit a lot of that to my mom. Growing up, I was a social person, and in the entertainment industry, that’s what [directors] were looking for, so it all worked out.”​

    Field Hockey Program Head Sue Hodgkins said that while working as an actress, her favorite part about being in the industry was working with the other people in her group.

    “I thought acting would be about creating something with a lot of people,” Hodgkins said. “Out of everything I’ve done, whether it was a television commercial, a film or a play, the best part is working with a bunch of people to create something that ends up being a collaborative project. A lot of the time, it always ends up being better than I thought it would be because of the suggestions and ideas other people bring up.”

    Hodgkins said acting required a specific set of emotional skills that she still relies on today.​

    “You have to be vulnerable and empathetic,” Hodgkins said. “You have to listen, connect with other people, have a wild curiosity about humanity and have a passion to be creative. That has never left me because once you do that, you just feel free.”

    Ella Temple ’27, who previously attended the school from seventh grade to 10th grade and has since transferred to Idyllwild Arts Academy, said dancing has also taught her skills off-stage.

    “Dancing has helped me find the confidence to make mistakes and allow myself to do that without it being harmful,” Temple said. “If you mess up, you just have to keep going and make sure your face doesn’t show it. It has helped me build confidence because a lot of the time, if I’m doing a complicated dance and I make a mistake, people don’t even realize it.”​

    Lane said the instincts she developed as an actor show up in her classroom while teaching her students.

    “I get to use my acting skills in the classroom,” Lane said. “There’s a feeling that comes up when you’re on stage or when you’re acting, where you can feel the energy in the room. I get the same energy from my students that I get from doing a play.”

    Temple said people often misunderstand what draws performers to the industry in the first place.

    “I’ve been very lucky in my community where I’ve had a lot of people that love theater for the humanity of it,” Temple said. “I’ve been fortunate to work in crowds that appreciate this form of the art, but I also have been in environments where people see acting as like having a spotlight. I perform for the passion of it and the hope of inspiring others and telling important stories that might change lives, rather than accolades.”

    Murphy said the key to surviving the harsh realities of the entertainment industry is for actors to love acting more than they want it to work out.

    “You have to remember why you act,” Murphy said. “You have to do it for the right reasons and enjoy the process of auditioning. You have to be happy, even if you don’t get the role, because chances are you’re not going to. It’s important for people to remember that if they’re doing it for the money, it’s not going to work out. There are so many actors and actresses out there that it’s better to connect with them than to try and compete.”

    This story was originally published on The Harvard-Westlake Chronicle on October 7, 2026.
